html:
The Roman law of 89 BCE that offered Roman citizenship to the people of Italy's allied communities. It was proposed by two tribunes, Marcus Plautius Silvanus and Gaius Papirius Carbo, in the middle of the Social War.

It built on the Lex Julia of 90 BCE, which had given citizenship to allied towns that stayed loyal or laid down their arms. The new law opened it to any man enrolled as a citizen of an allied town who lived in Italy and registered with a praetor in Rome within sixty days. A third law of the same year gave Latin rights to towns north of the Po.

The laws took the heart out of the revolt, though some Samnites fought on until 87 BCE. A fight followed over how the new citizens would vote: the Senate wanted to pack them into a few voting tribes, and the quarrel helped set off the clash between Marius and Sulla in 88 BCE.

In the long run Roman citizenship spread step by step. Julius Caesar extended it to the Po valley in 49 BCE, and in 212 CE the Constitutio Antoniniana gave it to almost every free person in the empire.
sum: The Roman law of 89 BCE that offered Roman citizenship to the people of Italy's allied communities. It was proposed by two tribunes, Marcus Plautius Silvanus and Gaius Papirius Carbo, in the middle of the Social War.
